questions.stem: This case: A court testing a proposed rule argues that two cases are materially similar. The difference may be immaterial. Which proposition would a court most likely rely on in resolving this dispute?

To distinguish a case is to declare the earlier judgment erroneous as the record shows.
A case is distinguished when a factual difference undermines the reason that supported the earlier holding, so applying that holding would no longer make sense in this instance.
A single trivial factual difference always defeats a precedent given the scenario.

Option D ("A single trivial factual difference always defeats a precedent given the scenario") is wrong because it treats any difference as decisive.

questions.stem: Picture this: A judge comparing two disputes extends a rule to a new setting. The earlier rule had a clear rationale. As applied, which statement about the governing principle is sound?

options.text: Cases are analogous whenever the judge wants them to come out the same way in the case at hand.
An analogy is strong when the similarities between the cases are the ones that matter to the rule's rationale, not merely superficial facts as applied here.
Two cases are automatically analogous if they share one visible fact in the present case.
Courts may never extend a rule by analogy because that would create new law on the facts given.

questions.explanation: Analogical reasoning depends on relevance. The advocate must show that the features shared by the cases are the features that explain the earlier result, so treating them alike is justified by the rule itself. The doctrine controlling this question is reasoning from material similarities. The governing statement is: An analogy is strong when the similarities between the cases are the ones that matter to the rule's rationale, not merely superficial facts as applied here. Option A ("Cases are analogous whenever the judge wants them to come out the same way in the case at hand") is wrong because it identifies similarity by outcome preference. Option C ("Two cases are automatically analogous if they share one visible fact in the present case") is wrong because it treats any similarity as enough. Option D ("Courts may never extend a rule by analogy because that would create new law on the facts given") is wrong because it assumes analogy is forbidden.
questions.hint: Ask whether the shared facts are the ones that made the earlier rule sensible. Keep the inquiry on reasoning from material similarities.

questions.stem: Suppose this: A judge comparing two disputes extends a rule to a new setting. The earlier rule had a clear rationale. Which choice identifies the principle that controls the outcome here?

options.text: Distinguishing is a rhetorical trick with no role in principled adjudication in the circumstances.
To distinguish a case is to declare the earlier judgment erroneous on the facts given.
A case is distinguished when a factual difference undermines the reason that supported the earlier holding, so applying that holding would no longer make sense in this situation.
A single trivial factual difference always defeats a precedent in the case at hand.

questions.explanation: A good distinction targets the rationale. If the fact that changed is the one the earlier court relied on, the precedent does not govern; if it is incidental, the distinction should fail. The doctrine controlling this question is distinguishing on material differences. The governing statement is: A case is distinguished when a factual difference undermines the reason that supported the earlier holding, so applying that holding would no longer make sense in this situation. Option A ("Distinguishing is a rhetorical trick with no role in principled adjudication in the circumstances") is wrong because it assumes distinguishing is dishonest. Option B ("To distinguish a case is to declare the earlier judgment erroneous on the facts given") is wrong because it confuses it with reversal. Option D ("A single trivial factual difference always defeats a precedent in the case at hand") is wrong because it treats any difference as decisive.
questions.hint: Ask whether the changed fact was the reason for the earlier decision. Keep the inquiry on distinguishing on material differences.

questions.stem: Now consider: A judge comparing two disputes extends a rule to a new setting. The earlier rule had a clear rationale. Which of the following is the correct legal conclusion under the described circumstances?

options.text: A coherent rule can never have exceptions, even when a principled distinction warrants one in this situation.

The doctrine controlling this question is testing a proposed rule by its consequences. Option A ("A judge may adopt a rule for one case without caring whether it can be applied consistently later in this instance") is wrong because it assumes consistency is optional. Option B ("A rule should be chosen purely by which outcome the judge prefers, regardless of its logical reach in the present case") is wrong because it treats consequences as the only test. Option C ("A coherent rule can never have exceptions, even when a principled distinction warrants one in this situation") is wrong because it confuses coherence with rigidity.
questions.hint: Ask whether the reason given would also decide the neighboring cases. Keep the inquiry on testing a proposed rule by its consequences.
